title: Sunglasses and Sun Protection Tips | Academy Vision
metaDescription: Sunglasses for the Jersey Shore: UV protection, polarized and tinted lenses, and warning signs worth a checkup. Tips from Academy Vision, Pine Beach, NJ.
h1: Choosing Sunglasses for Sun and Glare at the Jersey Shore
kicker: Squinting Into the Glare? Let’s Talk Sun Protection
lede: Between the river, the bay and the beaches, Pine Beach summers bring plenty of bright light bouncing off water and sand. Good sunglasses do more than stop the squint: they block ultraviolet (UV) light, tame glare and make long days outside more comfortable. Here’s what to look for, and when it’s worth talking with an eye doctor.

sections.heading: Start With UV Protection
sections.html:
The most important feature of a pair of sunglasses is the one you can’t see. Look for a label that says the lenses block 100% of UVA and UVB light, sometimes shown as UV400. A darker lens isn’t automatically safer: a dark tint without UV filtering lets your pupils open wider while UV still gets through.

Over many years, UV exposure has been linked to cataracts and to growths on the eye’s surface, and a single long day of reflected sun can leave eyes red, gritty and sore. Larger lenses and wraparound shapes help by blocking light that slips in around the edges, and a wide-brimmed hat adds even more shade.

sections.heading: Lens Choices for the Way You Spend Time Outside
sections.html:
• On the water or the sand: polarized lenses cut the bright glare that reflects off flat surfaces, which is why boaters, anglers and beachgoers tend to love them.
  • Behind the wheel: gray or brown lenses in a medium shade keep colors natural and traffic signals easy to read. Polarized lenses help with road glare, though they can make some dashboard and phone screens harder to see.
  • Golf, tennis and trail days: amber, rose or copper tints sharpen contrast, so a ball or the edge of a path stands out.
  • Sports and active kids: impact-resistant lenses, such as polycarbonate, in a frame that stays put.
  • In and out all day: light-adaptive lenses darken outdoors and clear indoors, but most darken less inside a car, because the windshield blocks much of the UV that triggers them.

Polarized lenses are one of the lens options we offer for eyeglasses at our Pine Beach optical, made for clearer vision outdoors.

sections.heading: Finding a Style You’ll Keep On
sections.html:
The right sunglasses are the ones you actually keep on. Aviators and rounded shapes suit many faces, wraparounds give the most coverage for sports and boating, and oversized frames shade more of the delicate skin around your eyes. Mirrored finishes cut extra brightness on the sunniest days. Whatever the shape, look for a snug, comfortable fit so you’re not pushing them back up every few minutes.

If you wear glasses, you have choices too: prescription sunglasses, clip-ons, or light-adaptive lenses in your everyday pair. Children need sun protection as much as adults, and often more, since they tend to spend more time outdoors.

sections.heading: Signs Your Eyes Need a Checkup
sections.html: Call an eye doctor if your eyes stay painful, red or very sensitive to light after a day in the sun, if bright light starts bothering you more than it used to, or if you notice a spot or growth on the white of the eye. Never look directly at the sun, even through dark sunglasses; an eclipse calls for certified eclipse viewers. If you lose vision suddenly or see a curtain or shadow over part of your vision, seek emergency care immediately.

sections.heading: More Ways to See Comfortably
sections.html: Sun protection is one part of the picture. Explore eyeglasses and lens options, browse designer frames, or read about contact lenses. Some contacts filter part of the UV, but no contact lens covers the whole eye and the skin around it, so sunglasses still matter.

faq.q: Do inexpensive sunglasses protect my eyes?
faq.a: They can. What protects your eyes is the UV rating on the label, not what you paid. Look for 100% UVA and UVB protection or UV400, and check that straight lines don’t wave or bend when you look through the lenses.

faq.q: Are polarized lenses better for my eyes?
faq.a: Polarization doesn’t add UV protection on its own, but it does cut reflected glare from water, sand and wet roads, which many people find much more comfortable. Check the UV label either way.
Yes, especially for long days at the beach or on the water. Choose a pair with full UV protection and impact-resistant lenses, in a size that stays on during play.

cta.heading: Have a Question About Sun Lenses?
cta.html: If you’d like to talk through sunglasses or sun lens options for your prescription, call Academy Vision at (732) 978-9306 and ask. And if it’s been a while since your last checkup, book an eye exam so any new lenses start from a current prescription.
